quests.title: Cave Painters
quests.story: Brrr, it's the Ice Age! Light your torch and step into a cave to discover how the very first people in Britain lived.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the torch with the right answer.
quests.hint: Think about a world with no farms or metal, only stone, bone, plants and wild animals.

questions.ask: What stone did Old Stone Age people chip to make sharp tools?
questions.fact: Toolmakers knocked flakes off flint to make hand axes with sharp, strong edges.

questions.ask: Where in England have Ice Age cave carvings been found?
questions.fact: In 2003, carvings of animals such as a deer and birds were spotted on the cave walls there.

questions.ask: Which famous cave in France is covered in Ice Age animal paintings?
questions.fact: Four teenagers and a dog found the Lascaux paintings in 1940.

questions.ask: What coloured earth did cave artists use to make red and yellow paint?
questions.fact: Black paint often came from charcoal, left over from their fires.

questions.ask: Why did Old Stone Age people move from place to place?
questions.fact: People who move around like this are called nomads.

questions.ask: Which huge, hairy animal did Ice Age people hunt?
questions.fact: Dinosaurs died out millions of years before any people lived.

questions.ask: What do we call people who hunt animals and gather wild plants?
questions.fact: They gathered berries, nuts, roots and shellfish as well as hunting.

questions.ask: What did fire help Old Stone Age people to do?
questions.fact: Fire also lit up dark caves and helped keep wild animals away.

questions.ask: What was the weather like at the coldest times of the Ice Age?
questions.fact: Thick sheets of ice covered much of Britain at the coldest times.

questions.ask: How did cave artists make outlines of their hands on the walls?
questions.fact: They may have blown paint through a hollow bone or reed onto the rock.

questions.ask: What did Old Stone Age people make their clothes from?
questions.fact: Needles made from bone were used to sew skins together.

questions.ask: These people did not write. How do we know how they lived?
questions.fact: Archaeologists study tools, bones and art to piece together how people lived.

quests.title: Skara Brae Storm

skill.name: Skara Brae, a New Stone Age village
skill.subject: history

quests.story: A wild storm has blown the sand away and uncovered a village of stone houses! Explore Skara Brae and find out who lived here.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the tablet with the right answer.
quests.hint: Remember these people were early farmers who lived by the sea, with very few trees around.

questions.ask: Where is the village of Skara Brae?
questions.fact: Orkney is a group of islands off the north coast of Scotland.

questions.ask: What uncovered Skara Brae in 1850?
questions.fact: Wind and huge waves stripped the grass and sand from a dune, showing the houses.

questions.ask: About how long ago did people live at Skara Brae?
questions.fact: That makes the village even older than the Great Pyramid in Egypt.

questions.ask: What was the furniture in the houses made from?
questions.fact: Orkney had few trees, so people built beds and shelves from flat stone slabs.

questions.ask: What was in the middle of each house?
questions.fact: The fire, or hearth, gave heat and light and was used for cooking.

questions.ask: Which stone furniture faced the door, maybe to show off special things?
questions.fact: A visitor would see the dresser first, so it may have held prized objects.

questions.ask: What did the people of Skara Brae sleep in?
questions.fact: The beds were probably filled with heather or bracken and furs to keep cosy.

questions.ask: How did the villagers get most of their food?
questions.fact: They kept cattle and sheep, grew barley and wheat, and gathered shellfish.

questions.ask: How were the houses joined to each other?
questions.fact: The houses were dug into mounds of old rubbish, called midden, to keep out the wind.

questions.ask: Which period of history is Skara Brae from?
questions.fact: The New Stone Age, or Neolithic, is when people in Britain began to farm.

questions.ask: What name is given to the patterned pots found at Skara Brae?
questions.fact: Grooved Ware pots have patterns of lines pressed or cut into the clay.

questions.ask: What were the tools at Skara Brae made from?
questions.fact: Beads and pins were carved from bone and even whale teeth.

quests.title: Stonehenge Sunrise
quests.story: The sun is rising over the great stones! Dig into the mysteries of Stonehenge and find out what we know, and what we still don't.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the mound with the right answer.
quests.hint: Remember the builders had no metal tools or machines, and some things about Stonehenge are still a mystery.

questions.ask: Where in England is Stonehenge?
questions.fact: Salisbury Plain is in Wiltshire, in the south of England.

questions.ask: About when did people begin building Stonehenge?
questions.fact: It began as a round ditch and bank, long before the big stones arrived.

questions.ask: What are the giant stones of Stonehenge called?
questions.fact: The sarsens came from West Woods, about 15 miles (25 km) to the north.

questions.ask: Where did the smaller bluestones come from?
questions.fact: They came from the Preseli Hills, around 150 miles (240 km) away!

questions.ask: Which sunrise does Stonehenge line up with?
questions.fact: It also lines up with the sunset on midwinter's day, the shortest day.

questions.ask: Do we know for certain why Stonehenge was built?
questions.fact: It may have been a temple, a calendar or a place to remember the dead.

questions.ask: Stonehenge was built in stages. About how long did that take?
questions.fact: Many generations of people added to it and changed its shape over time.

questions.ask: What did the builders use as picks to dig the ditch?
questions.fact: Archaeologists have found antler picks left in the bottom of the ditch.

questions.ask: How do many experts think the huge stones were moved?
questions.fact: No one knows for sure, but teams of people may have hauled sledges along wooden tracks.

questions.ask: Which nearby place may have been a village for Stonehenge's builders?
questions.fact: Lots of pig bones found there suggest big midwinter feasts.

questions.ask: What are the stones laid across the tops of the uprights called?
questions.fact: Lintels were fixed with joints like woodwork: a bump fitted into a hollow.

questions.ask: In which period of history was Stonehenge begun?
questions.fact: Its first builders used tools of stone, wood, bone and antler, not metal.

quests.title: Stone, Bronze or Iron?

skill.name: The Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age
skill.subject: history

quests.story: The museum's new crates have arrived, but the labels have fallen off! Help the curator put each find in the right age.
quests.instruction: Which age does it belong to? Tap the right crate.
quests.hint: Think about which material people had learned to use: stone came first, then bronze, then iron.

questions.ask: A flint hand axe
questions.fact: Hand axes were made by chipping flint into shape with another stone.

questions.ask: Hunting woolly mammoths
questions.fact: Woolly mammoths lived in Britain during the Ice Age.

questions.ask: The first farmers in Britain
questions.fact: Farming reached Britain around 4000 BC, in the New Stone Age.

questions.ask: The stone village of Skara Brae
questions.fact: Skara Brae was built around 3100 BC, before metal reached Britain.

questions.ask: A dagger made of bronze
questions.fact: Bronze is made by mixing copper with a little tin.

questions.ask: The Amesbury Archer
questions.fact: He was buried around 2300 BC with some of the earliest metal objects found in Britain.

questions.ask: Bell-shaped beaker pots
questions.fact: Beakers were often buried with people, perhaps holding a special drink.

questions.ask: Mining tin in Cornwall
questions.fact: Tin was rare, so Cornwall's tin was valuable for making bronze.

questions.ask: A sword made of iron
questions.fact: Iron was harder to work than bronze, but iron ore was easier to find.

questions.ask: Hillforts like Maiden Castle
questions.fact: Maiden Castle in Dorset is one of the biggest hillforts in Europe.

questions.ask: The first coins made in Britain
questions.fact: Some tribes made coins showing horses and the names of their leaders.

questions.ask: Ploughs tipped with iron
questions.fact: Strong iron tools helped farmers clear and plough more land.

quests.title: Hillfort Defenders
quests.story: Welcome to the hillfort! Grab a shield and join the tribe to discover how people lived high on the hill in the Iron Age.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the shield with the right answer.
quests.hint: Picture a tribe living in roundhouses inside high earth banks, with new iron tools to farm the land.

questions.ask: What was a hillfort?
questions.fact: Hillforts were protected by huge earth banks and deep ditches.

questions.ask: What is the name of the giant hillfort in Dorset?
questions.fact: Its earth banks surround an area bigger than 20 football pitches.

questions.ask: What shape were most Iron Age houses in Britain?
questions.fact: Roundhouses had a cone-shaped thatched roof and a fire in the middle.

questions.ask: What were roundhouse walls often made of?
questions.fact: Wattle is woven sticks; daub is a sticky mix of mud, straw and dung.

questions.ask: Which metal gave the Iron Age its name?
questions.fact: Iron ore was easier to find than copper and tin, so more people had metal tools.

questions.ask: Who were the religious leaders in Iron Age Britain?
questions.fact: Druids learned everything by heart, so much of what we know comes from Roman writers.

questions.ask: What is a torc?
questions.fact: The Snettisham hoard in Norfolk held dozens of beautiful gold and silver torcs.

questions.ask: What did some Iron Age warriors ride in?
questions.fact: Light chariots pulled by two small horses could race across the land.

questions.ask: What were the large groups of Iron Age people called?
questions.fact: Tribes included the Iceni in East Anglia and the Brigantes in the north.

questions.ask: What did some tribes start to make for buying and trading?
questions.fact: Some coins show the names of tribal leaders, such as Cunobelin.

questions.ask: What kind of languages did many Iron Age Britons speak?
questions.fact: Welsh, Cornish and Gaelic all grew from old Celtic languages.

questions.ask: Where did Iron Age farmers often store their grain?
questions.fact: Sealed pits kept grain dry and safe until it was time to sow it again.

quests.title: Journey Through Prehistory

skill.name: Britain from the Stone Age to the Iron Age in order
skill.subject: history

quests.story: Unroll the great scroll of time! Travel from the very first footprints in Britain all the way to the day the Romans arrived.
quests.instruction: Tap the event that happened longest ago first.
quests.hint: Remember the order of the ages: Stone Age, then Bronze Age, then Iron Age, then the Romans.

events.label: Happisburgh tools
events.fact: Flint tools and footprints at Happisburgh in Norfolk are the oldest signs of people in Britain.

events.label: Last Ice Age ends
events.fact: As the ice melted, forests grew and hunters followed deer and wild cattle into Britain.

events.label: Cheddar Man lives
events.fact: His skeleton, found in a Somerset cave, is Britain's oldest almost complete skeleton.

events.label: Britain is an island
events.fact: Rising seas flooded Doggerland, the land that once joined Britain to Europe.

events.label: Farming begins
events.fact: Farmers from Europe brought seeds and animals such as sheep and cattle.

events.label: Stonehenge begun
events.fact: It began as a round ditch and bank; the big stones came later.

events.label: Bronze Age begins
events.fact: People learned to mix copper and tin to make strong bronze.

events.label: Iron Age begins
events.fact: Iron tools and weapons slowly replaced bronze ones across Britain.

events.label: Romans invade
events.fact: Emperor Claudius sent an army, and Britain became part of the Roman Empire.

quests.title: Pyramid Builders
quests.story: The desert sun is blazing and the Great Pyramid towers above you! Join the builders and uncover the secrets of Giza.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the tablet with the right answer.
quests.hint: The Egyptians had no machines, so think what clever people could do with ropes, ramps and teamwork.

questions.ask: Who were the pyramids built for?
questions.fact: A pyramid was a tomb, built to protect the pharaoh's body and treasures.

questions.ask: Which pharaoh had the Great Pyramid built?
questions.fact: It was finished around 2560 BC and stayed the world's tallest building for over 3,800 years.

questions.ask: Where are the most famous pyramids in Egypt?
questions.fact: Giza is beside the River Nile, close to Egypt's capital city, Cairo.

questions.ask: Which giant statue at Giza has a lion's body and a human head?
questions.fact: The Great Sphinx was carved out of one huge lump of limestone rock.

questions.ask: Who do archaeologists think built the pyramids?
questions.fact: The workers' town has been found nearby, with bakeries and the workers' own tombs.

questions.ask: What stone was mostly used to build the Great Pyramid?
questions.fact: Smooth white limestone once covered the outside so it shone in the sun.

questions.ask: How were the heavy blocks probably raised up high?
questions.fact: Experts still debate whether the ramps were straight, zigzag or spiralling.

questions.ask: About how many stone blocks are in the Great Pyramid?
questions.fact: An average block weighs about 2.5 tonnes, as much as two cars.

questions.ask: What shape is the bottom (base) of a pyramid?
questions.fact: The Great Pyramid's sides face almost exactly north, south, east and west.

questions.ask: About how long did it take to build the Great Pyramid?
questions.fact: Thousands of workers took turns, with many coming to help when the Nile flooded.

questions.ask: On which side of the Nile were the pyramids built?
questions.fact: The Egyptians linked the west, where the sun set, with the land of the dead.

questions.ask: How did workers make it easier to drag blocks across sand?
questions.fact: An Egyptian painting shows a worker pouring water in front of a sledge.

quests.title: The Mummy Makers

skill.name: How the Ancient Egyptians made mummies
skill.subject: history

quests.story: The embalmers need an apprentice! Learn the steps the Egyptians followed to prepare a body for its journey to the afterlife.
quests.instruction: Tap the step the embalmers did first, then the next.
quests.hint: Think about it like a recipe: clean first, then dry, and finally wrap and protect.

events.label: Wash the body
events.fact: The body was washed with palm wine and water from the River Nile.

events.label: Remove the brain
events.fact: The Egyptians did not think the brain was needed in the afterlife, so it was not kept.

events.label: Remove the organs
events.fact: Embalmers took out the organs through a small cut in the left side.

events.label: Fill canopic jars
events.fact: Four canopic jars held the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines.

events.label: Leave the heart in
events.fact: The Egyptians believed the heart would be weighed in the afterlife.

events.label: Cover in natron
events.fact: Natron, a kind of salt, dried the body out over about 40 days.

events.label: Stuff and oil body
events.fact: Linen and sawdust filled out the shape, and oils kept the skin soft.

events.label: Wrap in linen
events.fact: Lucky charms called amulets were tucked between the layers of bandages.

events.label: Put on the mask
events.fact: The Egyptians believed the mask helped the spirit recognise its body.

events.label: Place in the coffin
events.fact: Important people had coffins inside a stone box called a sarcophagus.

quests.title: Tutankhamun's Treasure

skill.name: Tutankhamun and the discovery of his tomb
skill.subject: history

quests.story: It's 1922 in the Valley of the Kings, and a stone step has just been found! Dig with Howard Carter and discover the boy king's tomb.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the mound with the right answer.
quests.hint: Remember Tutankhamun was a young pharaoh, and his tomb lay hidden for over 3,000 years.

questions.ask: Who found Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922?
questions.fact: Carter had searched for years before his team uncovered the first step.

questions.ask: Where was Tutankhamun's tomb found?
questions.fact: Over 60 tombs have been found there, cut deep into the rocky hills.

questions.ask: About how old was Tutankhamun when he became pharaoh?
questions.fact: He became king around 1332 BC, which is why he is called the boy king.

questions.ask: About how old was Tutankhamun when he died?
questions.fact: No one knows for certain why he died so young; experts are still studying it.

questions.ask: Who paid for Howard Carter's search?
questions.fact: Lord Carnarvon was an English lord who loved Ancient Egypt.

questions.ask: Peering in by candlelight, what did Carter say he could see?
questions.fact: Gold glinted everywhere in the flickering light of his candle.

questions.ask: What is Tutankhamun's famous death mask mostly made of?
questions.fact: It weighs about 10 kg and is decorated with blue glass and precious stones.

questions.ask: Why was finding this tomb so exciting?
questions.fact: Robbers had broken in long ago, but most of the treasure was left behind.

questions.ask: About how many objects were found in the tomb?
questions.fact: It took Carter's team about ten years to record and clear them all.

questions.ask: In which country are Tutankhamun's treasures kept today?
questions.fact: Museums in Egypt look after the treasures, and millions of visitors come to see them.

questions.ask: What did the Egyptians believe the tomb's treasures were for?
questions.fact: The tomb held chariots, beds, board games and food for his next life.

questions.ask: What was Tutankhamun's innermost coffin made of?
questions.fact: He lay inside three coffins, one inside another, within a stone sarcophagus.

quests.title: Life on the Nile
quests.story: The great river is rising! Spend a year beside the Nile with farmers, scribes and priests, and earn gold coins as you learn.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the coin with the right answer.
quests.hint: Remember that almost everything in Egypt depended on the River Nile and its yearly flood.

questions.ask: What did the Nile's yearly flood leave behind on the fields?
questions.fact: The Egyptians called their land Kemet, 'the black land', after this rich soil.

questions.ask: How many seasons were there in the Egyptian farming year?
questions.fact: Each of the three seasons was about four months long.

questions.ask: What was the season of the Nile flood called?
questions.fact: Peret was the growing season and Shemu was harvest time.

questions.ask: What plant did the Egyptians use to make paper?
questions.fact: Papyrus reeds grew along the Nile; our word 'paper' comes from 'papyrus'.

questions.ask: What is Egyptian picture writing called?
questions.fact: There were hundreds of signs; some stood for sounds and some for whole words.

questions.ask: Which stone helped experts learn to read hieroglyphs?
questions.fact: It has one message in three scripts; Jean-François Champollion cracked it in 1822.

questions.ask: Who trained for years to read and write in Ancient Egypt?
questions.fact: Few Egyptians could write, so scribes were important and respected.

questions.ask: Who did the Egyptians believe was the god of the sun?
questions.fact: The Egyptians believed Ra sailed across the sky in a boat each day.

questions.ask: Which god with a jackal's head did Egyptians link with mummies?
questions.fact: The Egyptians believed Anubis guided the dead on their journey to the afterlife.

questions.ask: Which god did the Egyptians believe ruled the afterlife?
questions.fact: Osiris's wife, the goddess Isis, was known for her magic and protection.

questions.ask: What did Egyptian farmers grow to make bread and beer?
questions.fact: Workers were often paid in bread and beer instead of money.

questions.ask: What was the easiest way to travel a long way in Ancient Egypt?
questions.fact: Winds blew south, so boats could sail upstream and drift back north.
